tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>

schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

## F-25 — class loader lock on first load

- **Established:** On the compiled path, `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` takes the JDK's per-name class-loading lock (`getClassLoadingLock(name)`) for the whole load, the same way the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. So when several threads first use instantiations of generic code at once, the classes those instantiations need are made and loaded without a race.
- **Conditions:** The compiled path, the first load of an instantiation's class (a class the loader makes from a template), with threads running in parallel. Before the lock, two threads first-loading such classes at once could race and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (ledger row 417, now fixed). It was measured at four threads.
- **Consequence:** A worker can count on concurrent first loads being safe and need not add locking of their own; a change that removes or narrows the lock brings the NPE back. A change near the class loader's first load needs the four-thread atomic runs (`compiler.md` says so too).
- **Evidence:** `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG`, which calls a generic overload at eight instantiations inside a parallel `for`. At four threads it failed 5 of 5 runs without the lock and passed 5 of 5 with it. It is one of the gate's atomic runs (four threads; `gate.md` lists it). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 12.
- **Could not resolve:**

A declaration is "generic in its own right" if it is a generic function, a generic constructor, or a functional method with static parameters that sits in a trait or object that itself has none. Its declared domain (walk's "symbolic instance") is its parameter types with each type parameter left standing as a symbol bounded by its bounds. In all other cases, which include functional methods of a generic trait or object, walk compares the domains of the concrete instances the call creates. Generic dotted methods follow F-253 instead. Separately: if the chosen instance accepts an argument only after converting it (a coercion), walk converts it and dispatches again on the converted values, so the most specific declaration for them runs.

<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.

So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). 5	## F-7, "Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases"
6	
7	**Established:** Both ways of running a program go through the same parser and the same list of phases. The static type checker is one of those phases, but walk always has it off, and no option turns it on for walk. So under walk nothing checks the types of expressions before the program runs. A type error appears only when the faulty code runs, usually as a call for which no overload matches. Walk does check some declarations when it loads a program (overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, abstract methods that are inherited but never defined, `override`), and refuses the ones that break those checks. Only `fortress compile` runs the checker.

Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What remains: the `for` becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, a recursive split over boxed indices with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and each read and write of the mutable accumulator asks `BaseTask.inATransaction` (F-40). ## F-19

> - F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, a function call's arguments run in order (`CodeGen.evalArg`). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks, and both paths run every such block as a task: walk's library splits down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss`), and the compiler prelude's `parloop` stops at `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.

Meaning: scoped to the specification, with two limits settled from the code. The old entry stated the rule as what the tree does. The specification says that a program "must assume" parallel iterations (`for.tex`), that tuple elements, arguments and operands are evaluated "in parallel", and that an implementation may serialize them. The list now holds a call's arguments, which the record's text had left out; that is a closing of the list, not a change of the rule.

Second round:
- The first round said that both paths start a task only where they judge it worth it, after the sentence on loops. That holds for tuples, operands and arguments only. Loops split by `also do`, which both paths run as tasks with no such test. The entry now gives each mechanism. The specification's licence to serialize is now the reason that no program may count on parallel runs.
- The first round said that all parallelism in "the project's own programs" is implicit, since none writes `spawn` or `also`. The grep covers `explorations/` only, and the revival's tests write both. By the specification an `also do` block is itself implicit parallelism. The entry now bounds the grep and keeps `also do` with the implicit forms.
- Call arguments are restored to the title.

## F-22

> - F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".

Meaning: unchanged from the record; the first round's drop of "not codegen's" is undone in substance.
- The old title compared functions with variables. That comparison corrected a batch record, which had said that functions link. The current property is the lookup by the api's name, which the title now states.
- "The repository" meant the linker's component repository, not the git repository; it is now named.
- The by-hand mapping is restored. The text of 2026-10-13 had it ("only `LinkShell`'s `alink`/`clink` register another"); the cut of that day dropped it.

Second round:
- The first round dropped "not codegen's" and said that a fix can go on either side. The code says otherwise. Naming a reference after the api is the team's design, which the link step completes. `whoIsImplementingMyAPI` returns the api's name only when its maps hold nothing (`Linker.java:70-76`), and otherwise records a rewrite from the api to the implementer (`:79-88`). `linkMyComponent` applies the rewrites (`:222-250`), and `GraphRepository.getComponent` calls `Linker.linkAll()` (`GraphRepository.java:204`). So the missing step is the repository's, as the report says: "The name coincidence is the *repository's* assumption, not codegen's".
- The forwarder stays as the report's second repair, but walk and `fortress link` refuse before any code is generated, so they need the repository's repair.
- The `NoClassDefFoundError` now has its cause: the declaring class is named after the component (`CodeGen.java:394`), and the reference after the api (`NamingCzar.repairedApiName`, `NamingCzar.java:1673-1679`).
- "Reserved" is now "three comments leave a place", one of them `/* Need wrappers for the API, too. */`.

# What a size costs at run time, design A against design B

## The answers

- **Classes loaded (a), measured.** For the same program, the two designs load the same classes except the size's descriptors.
  - Per size of a generic, A loads two small descriptor classes, about 1.1 KB together.
  - B loads one holder class per distinct number, 300 bytes. Each stamped class that names the size is also about 120 bytes larger under B, because its initialiser passes the number's descriptor to a factory. That comes to about 660 bytes per size in these programs.
  - B has two fixed costs: the class `RTTIsize` once per program (1,204 bytes), and one descriptor pair per sized generic, about 2 KB, which is loaded twice, as the tree loads every descriptor class that is not stamped.
  - With one size, B loads 4 more classes and 4.7 KB more (pNat1: 2,343 classes against 2,339). With eight sizes of one generic, B loads 3 fewer classes and 1.5 KB more (SizedMany: 2,403 against 2,406). By these figures A loads fewer bytes up to about eleven sizes of one generic.
  - Either way the difference is a few kilobytes of the 8.6 MB of classes every run loads.
- **Start-up (a), measured.** Three runs each, interleaved: no difference beyond the machine's noise (pNat1: A 618, 583, 577 ms; B 598, 665, 571 ms).
- **The hot loop (b), measured.** A sized object's method, looping over its eight elements, called ten million times. The stamped method's bytecode is the same under both designs, line for line, and the size appears in it as the constant `ldc 8`. The times agree within 7 %, and which design is ahead flips between the two rounds of the same run. A loop bounded by the constant size is not measurably faster than the same loop bounded by the storage's length read at run time: the loop's cost is elsewhere, about 31 ns per element.
- **A call dispatched by size (c), measured.** For arms with literal sizes (`g(v: Vec[\RR64,3\])` beside `g(v: Vec[\RR64,4\])`), both designs compile the same dispatcher: one `instanceof` per arm on the stamped class, whose name holds the size. For an arm generic in a size (`f[\nat s\](v: Vec[\RR64,s\])`), only B picks the right arm; A picks the catch-all every time. B's dispatcher then reads the size's descriptor and looks the arm up in a table on every call. Against the same call resolved by the checker, a dispatched call costs about 4 to 20 ns more under either design, for literal arms and for B's size-generic arm alike. The loop itself costs 30 to 50 ns per call, and the same loop varies by up to 30 ns per call between runs.
- **Where a shape is checked (d), read from the code.**
  - At compile time, the first rung's checker refuses a size mismatch once per call site. The tree's checker does not.
  - At load time, nothing compares sizes. The loader only writes the arguments into names.
  - At a dispatched call, the size is tested on every call, once per arm tried.
  - At a type test, one `instanceof` per test.
  - At a call the checker resolved, nothing.
  - Per element inside a stamped method, nothing about the size. Each element read is the JVM's own array bounds check, whatever the size is.
  - Nothing today builds an optimisation on a size.
  - All of this is the same under A and B, except which dispatched arms work.

## 1. How it was measured

- **The stack.** `size-cost/run.sh` step `stack` calls `size-probes/run.sh <work-dir> build worlds`, which rebuilds the shadow stack from the committed patches into the work directory and compiles the compiler's prelude into four private caches. It then stamps B's per-number descriptor classes for 0 to 16 with the committed tool `java/StampSizeRTTI.java`. For the captures, those two commands were run by hand, as written in the step, before the step existed. On this container the stack and worlds took 9 min 2 s.
- **The two designs, each with all its measured pieces** (`run.sh:16-21, 48-49`):
  - A: `runtime/design-a.patch`, `runtime/value-position.patch`, `size-probes/fourth-gap-a.patch`, `size-probes/keep-size-params.patch`; world `cV`.

- F-40 **Measured on 2026-09-24 for two size designs that were not built, a size cost a few kilobytes at load and nothing in a hot loop, and only the overload dispatcher read a size off a value.** The two designs were design A, descriptor classes stamped for each size of each generic, and design B, a class for each number, passed to the generic's descriptor factory; both ran on the size probes' private build (`perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` section 1). The built design, one descriptor object per size value from `RTTIsize.of` (F-129), is neither, and nobody has measured its load size or its loops. Under either design, a size's classes came to a few kilobytes, against the 8.6 MB of classes that every run loads. A loop bounded by the size constant was not measurably faster than one bounded by the storage's length read at run time. The loop cost about 31 ns per element, which the bytecode shows going to a transaction check on each read and write of a local, to boxing, and to a method call for each element read. A call dispatched on a size cost about 4 to 20 ns more than the same call that the checker resolved at compile time. The built design's rung measured only the dispatcher's lookup of a literal size's descriptor: 0.9 ns on the landed build, its six runs from -2.2 to 7.0 ns, and 2.6 ns on an earlier build, on a dispatched call of about 23 ns. By reading the code of 2026-09-24, no optimization uses a size (F-20 holds it for today's tree), and a dispatched call tests a size once per overload arm tried, as the built dispatcher's literal leaf also does (`OverloadSet.java`, `SizeLiteralStructure`). Detail: `size-cost.md`, "The answers"; `compile-ladder/rung-size-runtime/REPORT.md` section 12.
- F-41 **The compiled dispatcher tests a size that two parameters share, in `DOT`'s shape, for equality in both directions before it chooses the arm that shares it.** `compiler_tests/NatRtDot` declares `dot[\nat n\](a: Vec[\RR64,n\], b: Vec[\RR64,n\])` over a user object `Vec`, beside a catch-all `dot(a: Any, b: Any)`. Sizes 3 and 4 reach the catch-all: typed statically, in the one order that the test makes, and dispatched at run time, in both orders. Walk printed the same in the probe. A static mismatch compiles with no error: the checker gives it the catch-all's signature. The dispatcher's equality test is the team's own check for a type variable in two invariant positions (`OverloadSet.java`). The library's `DOT` was not run compiled; by reading, the matrix product's shared inner size takes the same check. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtDot`, which checks the four outputs. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes.md` section 3.
- F-42 **The compiled checker skips a compilation unit's (an api's or a component's) overloading and return-type checks when an earlier stage of that unit has reported an error.** `StaticChecker` returns before `OverloadingChecker` if the earlier stages found errors (`StaticChecker.java:268-279`). So clearing an early error can raise the checker count, which sees only the errors before each unit's early return (F-53). The distance runs every stage of every unit whatever the earlier stages reported, so these errors are not hidden from it (`tools/distance/run.sh`, header). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/zero.md`, its opening section.
- F-43 **The overloading checker's memo hides some errors, and which ones changes from one build of the checker to another, so the gate's checker count and distance run with the memo off.** The memo keeps one verdict per pair of declarations, so a pair that several traits inherit is checked once, for the first trait in hash-set order (`perf-probes/nat/triage.md` section 1). The memo is on by default (`OverloadingChecker.scala:79`), so an ordinary `fortress compile` can miss these errors. The JVM property `-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false` turns it off; the gate's checker count and distance stages set it.
- F-44 **The compiled checker enforces the multiple instantiation exclusion rule and relies on it, and the one library meets the rule.** The rule: no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait. The checker's Return Type Rule relies on it: with the rule relaxed alone, a program passes the checker and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` (`OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`; the probe `ProbeMIEPick`). F-48 gives the kinds of static argument that the rule compares. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion: it accepts a type that extends two instantiations, and its overloading check does not count them as excluding (row 416; the review's section 3). P-43 keeps the rule. Besides the flat number tower of P-43, the library meets it by three changes of `952892a00`: `TotalComparison` extends `Comparison` and `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, no longer `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]`; `AnyMaybe` extends `AnyUniqueItem` alone, no longer `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` beside it; and `andCondCombine` chooses `andRelCond` by a `typecase`, in place of a second `ANDCOND`. So under walk, a program's `p1 ANDCOND p2` of two relational predicates, conditions built from a relation over a generator, which `filter` fuses, is no longer itself a relational predicate (row 458). The distance holds no exclusion error (F-53). Detail: `reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` sections 1 to 3; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:121-123`, `:959`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4861-4867`.
- F-45 **Without the exclusion rule, every dispatcher would have to call its generic arms at the call site's static arguments, and no published work resolves a value that is in two instantiations of one generic under run-time dispatch.** The loader already gives a generic dispatcher the call site's static arguments; without the rule, its arms would have to use them instead of arguments read from the value (`reviews/mie-probes/scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3). The call at the dispatcher's static arguments is built for template dispatchers (F-136), and, by reading, not for one with an `opr` or `nat` static parameter (`compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` section 9). The team's 2012 patents allow a self-typed generic, one that comprises exactly its parameter, at several instantiations along a chain of subtypes: the forest rule (`reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md` section 1). Alone, the forest rule leaves the specialisation hole open: a specialised declaration, more specific than the generic one, runs for a value at a narrower level of the chain, a subtype, and returns a type that a caller typed at that narrower level does not expect. Compiled under a shadow checker with the forest rule, a patched copy of the checker that never landed, such a run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`; the tree's checker refuses such a program (the same note, section 3). Route C adds a return-type rule that closes the hole (F-46). Detail: `scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3; `reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`, "What the field settled and what it did not".

Built as a shadow checker on 2026-09-24 and run through the zero probe's stack on a library copy without the reduction markers, route C refuses 25 pairs at 21 of the nested tower's declarations: specialisations that a level below does not cover. Completing the tower needs seven more declarations and the identification of `Integral[\ZZ32\]` with `ZZ32`. The patents' `comprises T` on the self-typed traits licenses that identification, but it overflows the checker's stack (measured on the zero probe's copy of the checker, in the recursion of `Formula.scala` that the tree shares). A hierarchy check of its own could enforce the identification instead; none is built. Leaving route A for route C also needs: the tower nested again; the call-site fix in every dispatcher (F-136); in the code generator, a method for each middle level of a chain, whose absence, by the error text, makes such a chain die with `AbstractMethodError`; walk to accept the specialised pairs without overflowing on `comprises T`; and, for the identification, a way past the checker's overflow or the hierarchy check. Detail: `reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md` sections 2 to 5.
- F-47 **The exclusion rule refuses some of the specification's own examples; in their place, a parametric object with a factory, or a widening function, runs on both paths as a user program.** The refused examples are E1 to E10 of `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, "What was found": among them three `where`-clause examples, the Working Draft's `Nothing`, the nested number tower and `RationalQuantity`. The `where`-clause examples stop on both paths before the rule, in name resolution, at `T is undefined`. The alternatives were measured as user programs that declare their own types: a parametric object with a factory, such as `object Empty[\T\]` with `emptyList[\E\]()`, and a widening function, such as `widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\]`. The library's `Nothing[\String\]` does not yet run on the compiled path's prelude (row 331, F-167). A marker object with a `coerce` in the generic trait, as `AltEmptyCoerce` has in `SList[\T\]`, also runs compiled, and walk applies such a coercion (row 389). The 2012 `covariant` keyword passes the compiled checker and dies at run time (row 404). The compiled checker refuses a coercion with its own static parameter between two instantiations, `coerce[\S extends T\](c: C[\S\])`, as a cyclic hierarchy. Inferred from the forest rule: route C (F-46) would rescue neither the `where`-clause examples, `Nothing` nor E8, the internal appendix's "Disjunctive Constraints"; only the tower (E5) and the root `Object`'s algebra (E7) would keep their original text under it. Detail: the same note.

Nor does a static parameter beside another argument: `object O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` passes the checker and dies at load with `ClassFormatError` (row 414, `XXXNatExtendsTwice`; the row also places its cause in `TypeHierarchyChecker`'s check of `extends` clauses). The compiled checker refuses such a pair under the bound `Any`: a functional whose one parameter has a parametric type bounded by `Any` cannot be overloaded (the probe `FillBoxAny`). The distance runs every stage of every unit whatever the earlier stages reported, so these errors are not hidden from it (`tools/distance/run.sh`, header). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/zero.md`, its opening section.
+- F-43 **The overloading checker's memo hides some errors, and which ones changes from one build of the checker to another, so the gate's checker count and distance run with the memo off.** The memo keeps a "valid" verdict per pair of declarations. A pair that several traits inherit is checked once per trait, at that trait's instantiation, in hash-set order, so a pair valid for one trait is taken as valid for the next (`perf-probes/nat/triage.md` section 1). The memo is on by default (`OverloadingChecker.scala:79`), so an ordinary `fortress compile` can miss these errors. The JVM property `-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false` turns it off; the gate's checker count and distance stages set it.
+- F-44 **The compiled checker enforces the multiple instantiation exclusion rule and relies on it, and the one library meets the rule.** The rule: no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait. The checker's Return Type Rule relies on it: with the rule relaxed alone, a program passes the checker and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` (`OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`; the probe `ProbeMIEPick`). F-48 gives the kinds of static argument that the rule compares. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion: it accepts a type that extends two instantiations, and its overloading check does not count them as excluding (row 416; the review's section 3). P-43 keeps the rule. Besides the flat number tower of P-43, the library meets it by three changes of `952892a00`: `TotalComparison` extends `Comparison` and `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, no longer `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]`; `AnyMaybe` extends `AnyUniqueItem` alone, no longer `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` beside it; and `andCondCombine` chooses `andRelCond` by a `typecase`, in place of a second `ANDCOND`. So under walk, a program's `p1 ANDCOND p2` of two relational predicates, conditions built from a relation over a generator, which `filter` fuses, is no longer itself a relational predicate (row 458). The distance holds no exclusion error (F-53). Detail: `reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` sections 1 to 3; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:121-123`, `:959`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4861-4867`.
+- F-45 **Without the exclusion rule, every dispatcher would have to call its generic arms at the call site's static arguments, and no published work resolves a value that is in two instantiations of one generic under run-time dispatch.** The loader already gives a generic dispatcher the call site's static arguments; without the rule, its arms would have to use them instead of arguments read from the value (`reviews/mie-probes/scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3). The call at the dispatcher's static arguments is built for template dispatchers (F-136), and, by reading, not for one with an `opr` or `nat` static parameter (`compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` section 9). The team's 2012 patents allow a self-typed generic, one that comprises exactly its parameter, at several instantiations along a chain of subtypes: the forest rule (`reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md` section 1). Alone, the forest rule leaves the specialisation hole open: a specialised declaration, more specific than the generic one, runs for a value at a narrower level of the chain, a subtype, and returns a type that a caller typed at that narrower level does not expect. Compiled under a shadow checker with the forest rule, a patched copy of the checker that never landed, such a run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`; the tree's checker refuses such a program (the same note, section 3). Route C adds a return-type rule that closes the hole (F-46). Detail: `scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3; `reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`, "What the field settled and what it did not".
+- F-46 **Route C, the patents' forest rule with a return-type rule over every level of a chain, closes the specialisation hole (F-45), but going back to a nested number tower under it needs work beyond the checker.** The library's tower was nested before route A flattened it (P-43). Built as a shadow checker on 2026-09-24 and run through the zero probe's stack on a library copy without the reduction markers, route C refuses 25 pairs at 21 of the nested tower's declarations: specialisations that a level below does not cover. Completing the tower needs seven more declarations and the identification of `Integral[\ZZ32\]` with `ZZ32`. The patents' `comprises T` on the self-typed traits licenses that identification, but it overflows the checker's stack (measured on the zero probe's copy of the checker, in the recursion of `Formula.scala` that the tree shares). A hierarchy check of its own could enforce the identification instead; none is built. Leaving route A for route C also needs: the tower nested again; the call-site fix in every dispatcher (F-136); in the code generator, a method for each middle level of a chain, whose absence, by the error text, makes such a chain die with `AbstractMethodError`; walk to accept the specialised pairs without overflowing on `comprises T`; and, for the identification, a way past the checker's overflow or the hierarchy check. Detail: `reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md` sections 2 to 5.
+- F-47 **The exclusion rule refuses some of the specification's own examples; in their place, a parametric object with a factory, or a widening function, runs on both paths as a user program.** The refused examples are E1 to E10 of `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, "What was found": among them three `where`-clause examples, the Working Draft's `Nothing`, the nested number tower and `RationalQuantity`. The `where`-clause examples stop on both paths before the rule, in name resolution, at `T is undefined`. The alternatives were measured as user programs that declare their own types: a parametric object with a factory, such as `object Empty[\T\]` with `emptyList[\E\]()`, and a widening function, such as `widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\]`. The library's `Nothing[\String\]` does not yet run on the compiled path's prelude (row 331, F-167). A marker object with a `coerce` in the generic trait, as `AltEmptyCoerce` has in `SList[\T\]`, also runs compiled, and walk applies such a coercion (row 389). The 2012 `covariant` keyword passes the compiled checker and dies at run time (row 404). The compiled checker refuses a coercion with its own static parameter between two instantiations, `coerce[\S extends T\](c: C[\S\])`, as a cyclic hierarchy. Inferred from the forest rule: route C (F-46) would rescue neither the `where`-clause examples, `Nothing` nor E8, the internal appendix's "Disjunctive Constraints"; only the tower (E5) and the root `Object`'s algebra (E7) would keep their original text under it. Detail: the same note.
+- F-48 **The compiled checker's exclusion rule compares type arguments, and sizes only when both are literals.** Two boolean arguments count as no exclusion: `object F extends { Flag[\true\], Flag[\false\] }` passes the checker and dies in code generation (row 406, `compiler_tests/XXXBoolExtendsTwice`). Nor does a static parameter beside another argument: `object O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` passes the checker and dies at load with `ClassFormatError` (row 414, `XXXNatExtendsTwice`; the row also places its cause in `TypeHierarchyChecker`'s check of `extends` clauses). Two literal sizes do exclude: the checker refuses `object V extends { Vec[\3\], Vec[\4\] }`, "Types Vec[\3\] and Vec[\4\] exclude each other" (row 402, fixed). Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNatExcludeChecker`, for the refusal of two literal sizes. The code is `TypeAnalyzer.scala:539-546`, "Todo: Handle bool args". Detail: `reviews/spec-refused-examples-judgement.md` section 6.
+- F-49 **Under walk, a value form and a function form of one name are chosen by the argument's run-time type, so with the element type `Any` a function passed as the value goes to the function form.** Given a function, `fill` on an array of element type `Any` stored the function's results, `c[1] = 11`, not the function. The compiled checker refuses such a pair under the bound `Any`: a functional whose one parameter has a parametric type bounded by `Any` cannot be overloaded (the probe `FillBoxAny`). The one library has no such pair: `fill` takes a value and `tabulate` a function (F-158). Detail: `reviews/fill-overloads-ways.md` section 2.
+- F-50 **The compiled checker lets overloads differ in static parameters, as the model of the OOPSLA 2011 paper does, which the specification now states (F-174); as ambiguous, it refuses only the pairs it cannot prove unambiguous.** It builds P-45. It cannot prove a pair over open traits, which no `excludes` or `comprises` clause closes, nor one whose domains exclude only through the exclusion rule and a bound, as the library's `CAP` on `ScalarRange[\I\]` beside `Range2D[\I,J\]` does. It also refuses some pairs that the paper accepts, by its Return Type Rule and by its positional rule, under which two generic declarations in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters by position (F-75). Other gaps have their own owners: its overloading check never reads a pair of symbolic operators such as `+` (P-155, row 584); two generic arms on a bare type variable fail compiled (F-174, row 537); and walk runs an arm whose size the call leaves unfixed, with the size unbound, where the checker drops the arm or refuses the call (F-69, row 400). Detail: `reviews/overload-static-params-ways.md` sections 2 and 3.
+- F-51 **A generic call converts a narrower argument for a parameter typed by a type variable that another argument fixes, on both paths.** For `scale[\T\](b: Box[\T\], x: T)` and `b: Box[\RR64\]`, `scale(b, 3)` takes `T = RR64` and converts the `3` (row 388, fixed). So under walk the library's array-scalar `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX`, and the matrix-scalar juxtaposition and `DOT`, take a `ZZ32` scalar with `RR64` elements. F-73 and F-137 give each path's rule. Gated by `tests/InferCoercionRungK` and `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes`. Detail: `reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review/row388-container-probe.md`.
+- F-?1 **The compiled checker refuses a local function's parameter that has no type, "Missing parameter type for i", as it refuses a top-level function's.** Write the type: the specification asks for inference of a type that a declaration leaves out, and does not describe it (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, "The type of a parameter that a declaration leaves out"). Before the fix, such a local function crashed the checker (rows 620 and 621, fixed). Row 405 holds the case elsewhere: compiled, an untyped parameter is refused wherever it appears; under walk, it fails only when its method implements an abstract declaration. Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXLocalFunctionUntypedParam` and `XXXLocalFunctionUntypedParamInLoop`. The code is `STypeEnv.scala:75` (local) and `:200` (top level).
+- F-?2 **The compiled checker refuses a subtrait that inherits an abstract method named by an operator static argument, even at one instantiation; the specification and walk substitute the name.** The abstract-method check matches an inherited abstract method to a concrete one by name, and does not first put in the operator argument (`AbstractMethodChecker.scala:100-101`, by reading). Observed in the probes `OprSingle` and `OprInstancesOplus`; no ledger row or test holds it. Detail: `reviews/spec-refused-examples-judgement.md` section 4.
+- F-?3 **The code generator throws on `Any` as a static argument in an `extends` clause, after the checker has accepted the program.** It stops with "Only handling some static args of generic types in extends clause" (`CodeGen.java:5805`). Observed in the probe `AltEveryContra`; no ledger row or test holds it. Detail: `reviews/spec-refused-examples-judgement.md` sections 3.1 and 9.
